s: God tells Jeremiah that he will destroy Jerusalem for its sins. Jeremiah begs that the city not fall into the hands of the Chaldeans, and God promises that his angels will open the gates themselves.
Jeremiah and Baruch mourn in the Temple. Jeremiah sends Abimelech the Ethiopian to fetch figs from the vineyard of Agrippa.
At night the angels come with torches. Jeremiah buries the Temple vessels in the earth, and God tells him to go to Babylon with the people and Baruch to stay behind.
The angels open the walls and the Chaldeans enter the city. Jeremiah throws the Temple keys up to the sun, and a hand takes them. Baruch weeps over Jerusalem and stays at a tomb.
Abimelech falls asleep under a tree and wakes sixty-six years later, his figs still fresh. Confused, he finds that the city has changed, and an old man tells him what has happened.
An angel leads Abimelech to Baruch. Seeing the fresh figs, Baruch praises God for this sign of the resurrection and writes a letter to Jeremiah in Babylon.
An eagle carries the letter and figs to Babylon. It lands on a dead man at a funeral and he comes to life. Jeremiah reads the letter and the people prepare to return.
Jeremiah leads the people out of Babylon, but those who will not leave their foreign spouses are turned away from Jerusalem and build Samaria.
Jeremiah offers sacrifice and seems to die, then revives and prophesies the coming of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. The people stone him, and Baruch and Abimelech bury him.
i: 4 Baruch, also called the Paralipomena of Jeremiah or The Rest of the Words of Baruch, is a short book written around AD 120 to 140, after the Romans had destroyed Jerusalem a second time. It looks back to the first destruction, by the Babylonians, and asks the same question: will God ever bring his people home?

It tells three stories. Before the city falls, Jeremiah hides the Temple vessels in the earth and hands its keys to the sun. Abimelech the Ethiopian, who once saved Jeremiah from the pit (Jeremiah 38), is sent to fetch figs and falls asleep for sixty-six years, waking to find the figs still fresh: a sign that the dead will rise. Then an eagle carries letters between Baruch in Jerusalem and Jeremiah in Babylon, and the exiles return.

The book ends with Jeremiah’s death in the Temple, his prophecy of Jesus the Son of God, and his stoning. The Ethiopian Church reads it as Scripture; the Catholic Church does not count it among the books of the Bible.
